newsitem.title: CHINA: China says human rights cloak for power politics.
newsitem.headline: China says human rights cloak for power politics.

text.p: China, under fire for human rights abuses, on Thursday accused "some people" of using human rights as a cloak for power politics and said the concept of human rights differed between cultures.

"Some people may be used to passing judgments on issues of human rights from an abstract and biased understanding that has been acquired on the basis of a human rights conception of their own region," the China Daily said in a commentary.

Several small nations had come under pressure from people claiming to uphold human rights but secretly working to impose their own values, said the commentary by Fan Guoxiang, vice-chairman of the China Society for Human Rights Studies.
"We want an impartial universality of human rights. We do not want disguised power politics covered with a cloak of human rights," the commentary said.
Attempts to impose one set of values on another country were often counter-productive, it said.
Although the commentary did not name the United States directly, it took obvious swipes at Washington over its human rights spats with other nations.

"In the name of the 'rule of law' they never hesitate to impose sanctions on many countries having trade ties with a small nation on the basis of a congressional act," it said in an apparent reference to Cuba.
U.S. President Bill Clinton in March enacted a law aimed at discouraging foreign firms from conducting business in Cuba.

In apparent criticism of Washington's reaction to Singapore's 1994 caning of an American youth convicted of vandalism, the commentary said: "They do not care to listen to the rule of law of another small nation that stands firm on the legitimate punishment of a foreign young hooligan."
Clinton had criticised the punishment as extreme.

The article also appeared to slam U.S.-led intervention in Haiti in 1995 that ousted the country's military junta as a distortion of human rights under the pretence of humanitarian intervention and restoration of democracy.
China has come under heavy fire from international human rights groups that accuse Beijing of rampant human rights abuses. Beijing vehemently denies such charges.
Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen and U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher met in New York on Wednesday to discuss human rights and other issues.
